data.hypothesis: A six-way scalar unroll tests whether a moderate number of independent minimum/index chains can approach the measured two- and eight-accumulator results while avoiding the overhead that may have hurt three and four accumulators. It may help most on decreasing inputs, where each lane's minimum is repeatedly updated; on random inputs, extra comparisons and the final fold may outweigh reduced loop-carried dependence. Prior measurements are aggregate, so per-pattern outcomes remain to be checked after correctness validation.

memory_lessons.applicability: Use these results to choose contrasting unroll factors, not to assume performance scales with accumulator count.
memory_lessons.claim: The two-accumulator candidate measured 2.2604 µs, the eight-accumulator candidate 2.2920 µs, and the three- and four-accumulator candidates 3.0152 µs and 2.8135 µs respectively. The observed aggregate results do not show a monotonic benefit from more accumulators.
memory_lessons.next_experiment: Measure this six-accumulator candidate with correctness checks and report random and decreasing input timings separately.

data.notes: Historical candidates were reported valid and correct, with five correctness cases each. Their supplied timings are aggregate means, so they do not establish which factor is faster on random versus decreasing inputs. The supplied target facts are AMD EPYC 9654, GCC 14.2, x86_64, one core. This proposal uses scalar comparisons only and makes no performance claim before controller measurement.
transformations: Replaced the single-chain scan with a fixed six-way scalar scan using six independent minimum-value and index accumulators.
Folded the six results using signed minimum-value comparison and lowest-index tie-breaking.
Handled inputs smaller than six with a scalar scan and processed any remaining elements scalarly after the fold.
Used no explicit SIMD and no parallel workers.
